floors.name: Threshold of Syntax
floors._readme_concepts: Every concept here needs at least 2 practice challenges tagged to it, or validation fails.

lesson._readme: 2 to 4 sections. One idea each. Every section needs a code example AND a checkpoint - the checkpoint is the gate to the next section.

sections.title: Variables and Assignment
sections.body:
A **variable** is a name pointing at a value. You create one with `=`, which is not equality - it means store this value under this name.

Read it right to left: evaluate the right side, then bind the name on the left.

Keep this to 3-5 sentences. If it needs more, it is two sections.

annotations.text: score now refers to the integer 42.
The right side is computed first, then stored back into score.

checkpoint._readme: One task, directly about what this section just showed. No id, no xp, no tags - a checkpoint is not a graded challenge.
checkpoint.prompt: Assign the value 100 to a variable called `score` and print it.
checkpoint.hint1: Use the = operator to assign a value.
checkpoint.hint2: The variable name goes on the left: score = ...

sections.title: Second Idea
sections.body: The second concept for this floor. Note the `{{link:algorithms}}` syntax is available for inline concept links into another dungeon - the target id must exist in index.json.
sections.code:
total = 0
for n in [1, 2, 3]:
    total = total + n
print(total)

annotations.text: Each pass adds the next value to the running total.

checkpoint.prompt: Store the sum of 5, 10 and 15 in a variable called `total`. Do not print anything.
checkpoint.hint1: You can add the three numbers directly.

practice._readme: 6 to 10 challenges. Every one must pass before the exam opens. Escalate: the first is near-trivial, the last combines every idea on the floor.
practice.prompt: Write a function `add(a, b)` that returns the sum of its two arguments.
practice.explain: Returning rather than printing lets the caller use the result in another expression. A function that only prints hands back None.

practice._readme: input is the ARGUMENTS as source text; expected is a real JSON value. Comparison is structural, so 30 matches 30.0.
practice.prompt: Write `largest(a, b, c)` returning the biggest of its three arguments. Do not use the built-in `max`.
practice.explain: Tracking a best-so-far value scales to any number of inputs, where chained comparisons stop being readable after three.

practice._readme: A whole-program challenge has no fn; input is then stdin and expected is the printed output.
practice.prompt: Read a name from input and print exactly `Well met, <name>.`
practice.explain: input() always returns a string, so no conversion is needed here - but it would be if you did arithmetic on it.

practice.prompt: This should let its result be used in arithmetic, but the call crashes. Fix it.
practice.explain: print shows a value to a human; return hands one back to the caller. Only one of those can be added to something.
practice.hint: The function shows the answer but never gives it back.

practice.prompt: Write `double_all(numbers)` returning a new list with every number doubled.
practice.explain: Building a new list leaves the caller's data untouched. Mutating the argument in place would surprise whoever passed it.

practice.prompt: Write `summarise(numbers)` returning the total of a list of numbers.
practice.explain: Starting the accumulator at 0 is what makes the empty case fall out correctly instead of needing a special branch.

exam._readme: 8 to 12 questions, 80% to pass. Mix the types, but keep at least half of them code-writing.
exam.prompt: What is the type of the value `3.0`?
exam.explain: A decimal point makes it a float even when the fractional part is zero. int and float are distinct types with different behaviour on division.
Each line rebinds the name using its current value, so the multiplication uses 2, not the original literal.

exam.prompt: This crashes with a TypeError. Fix it without changing `level`.
exam.explain: You cannot join a str and an int with +. str(level) converts it; an f-string does the same thing more readably.

exam.prompt: Write `clamp(x, low, high)` returning `low` if `x` is below it, `high` if above, otherwise `x`.
exam.explain: Returning early on each bound reads better than one nested conditional, and makes the inclusive boundary case obvious.

exam.prompt: Write `count_words(sentence)` returning how many words it contains. An empty string has 0 words.
exam.explain: split() with no argument collapses runs of whitespace and drops empty results, which is why the empty string gives 0 rather than 1.
range(1, 4) yields 1, 2 and 3 - the stop value is never produced.

exam.prompt: A function body runs to the end without hitting a `return`. What does the call evaluate to?
exam.explain: Python returns None implicitly. That is why calling a print-only function and using its result gives None rather than the printed text.

exam.prompt: Write `initials(first, last)` returning the two first letters uppercased and joined by a dot: `initials("mira", "vale")` gives `"M.V"`.
exam.explain: Indexing with [0] takes the first character; .upper() normalises input you do not control, so the output is consistent either way.
